conceptBreakdown.content:
### 1.1 EFB Definition of Biotechnology
- According to the **European Federation of Biotechnology (EFB)**:
  > *"Biotechnology is the integration of natural science and organisms, cells, parts thereof, and molecular analogues for products and services."*
- This definition encompasses both traditional microbial fermentation techniques (curd, wine, bread) and modern recombinant DNA technology.

### 1.2 Two Core Pillars of Biotechnology
1. **Genetic Engineering**:
   - Techniques used to chemically alter, synthesize, and transfer genetic material (DNA and RNA) into a recipient host organism, stably altering the host's phenotype.
   - Involves restriction cleavage, vector ligation, and host transformation to produce **Recombinant DNA (rDNA)** molecules.
2. **Bioprocess Engineering**:
   - Creation and maintenance of strictly sterile, aseptic microbial conditions in large-scale chemical engineering reactors (bioreactors).
   - Ensures that only the desired transformed microorganism or cell line grows in high density, uncontaminated by wild competitor species, to harvest pure enzymes, antibiotics, and therapeutic proteins.

conceptBreakdown.heading: Historical Emergence of rDNA Technology
conceptBreakdown.title: Historical Emergence of rDNA Technology
conceptBreakdown.content: Stanley Cohen and Herbert Boyer (1972) constructed the first recombinant DNA molecule by isolating an antibiotic resistance gene from Salmonella typhimurium and ligating it into a native plasmid vector using restriction endonucleases and DNA ligase.

conceptBreakdown.heading: Aseptic Engineering Invariants
conceptBreakdown.title: Aseptic Engineering Invariants
conceptBreakdown.content: Aseptic engineering utilizes HEPA air filtration, steam sterilization (autoclaving at 121°C and 15 psi), and positive pressure barriers to prevent airborne contaminant spores from entering industrial fermentation vessels.
